title: Building a Puzzle from Lines
concept_layer: lines as construction tool, perpendicularity, dot product as geometry test

capture_leaks.euclidean_assumption: foundationscrisis — perpendicularity assumes flat space; non-Euclidean geometry breaks this
capture_leaks.exact_orthogonality: randomness, machinelearning — real systems are approximately perpendicular; tolerance hides deep complexity
capture_leaks.semantic_independence: machinelearning — mathematical ⊥ is not conceptual ⊥; feature orthogonality in ML is a different beast
capture_leaks.two_dimensional_reasoning: Point_Triangle, fractals — lines cross in pairs; three lines make area, many make recursion
capture_leaks.static_constraint: forces, softbodies — these lines cannot bend or respond; rigid geometry is the corpse of living structure

limit: These lines cross but do not yield. They are perpendicular in flat space only. Every tolerance you accept hides a paradox. Every constraint you satisfy defers a deeper question. The puzzle solves. The ontology does not.
description: In Point_Line you built one line. Now lines become tools — arrange them to form shapes, and the code validates whether your construction is geometrically correct.

stages.title: One line is a relation. Two lines are a question.
stages.thinking: In Point_Line, a single line connected two points. Now there are two lines, four endpoints, and a question: can you arrange them into a plus sign? Lines stop being measurements and become building material. The question is geometry — the answer is your hands.

stages.title: Define where the answer lives
stages.thinking: The puzzle needs target positions — the places where endpoints must land for the shape to be correct. Four glowing markers in a cross pattern. The targets are the answer written in space, waiting for the player to discover them by snapping lines into place.
stages.code:
extends LineSnapPuzzleBase
class_name PlusLinePuzzle

func _init() -> void:
	# The 4 target vertices for + shape
	target_positions = [
		Vector3(0, 0, -0.2),   # Center-back
		Vector3(0, 0, 0.2),    # Center-front
		Vector3(0, -0.2, 0),   # Bottom-center
		Vector3(0, 0.2, 0)     # Top-center
	]
	
	# Where lines start before the player moves them
	line_start_positions = [
		[Vector3(0.2, -0.25, -0.15), Vector3(0.2, -0.25, 0.15)],
		[Vector3(0.2, -0.4, -0.15), Vector3(0.2, -0.4, 0.15)]
	]

stages.title: Build the base class
stages.thinking: PlusLinePuzzle extends LineSnapPuzzleBase. This is the first time we see class inheritance — a base class that handles all the shared puzzle logic (creating markers, managing snap, checking completion) while the specific puzzle only defines its targets and constraints. Write the common parts once, specialize many times.
stages.code:
extends Node3D
class_name LineSnapPuzzleBase

## Puzzle Configuration
@export var auto_validate: bool = true
@export var show_target_markers: bool = true
@export var lock_on_complete: bool = true

## Internal state
var target_positions: Array[Vector3] = []
var line_start_positions: Array[Array] = []
var form_constraints: Array[FormConstraint] = []
var snap_lines: Array[SnapLineSegment] = []
var is_completed: bool = false

## Signals
signal puzzle_completed()
signal line_snapped_to_target(line: SnapLineSegment)

func _ready() -> void:
	if target_positions.is_empty():
		push_error("target_positions not set!")
		return
	
	await get_tree().process_frame
	call_deferred("_setup_target_markers")
	call_deferred("_setup_lines")

stages.title: Holographic target markers
stages.thinking: Each target position gets a glowing marker — a torus ring with emission, styled after Half-Life: Alyx’s holographic puzzles. Cyan glow, small radius, visible from any angle. These are not decorative — they are the affordance that tells the player "snap here."

stages.title: The perpendicularity test
stages.thinking: How does the code know two lines form a plus? The dot product. Two direction vectors with dot product zero are perpendicular — 90 degrees between them. This is the first time algebra defines geometry: a number (zero) means a shape (right angle). The constraint system checks this automatically when endpoints snap.

stages.title: Snap and validate
stages.thinking: When a line endpoint gets close enough to a target marker, it snaps — position jumps to the exact target. After every snap, the system checks: are all endpoints at targets? Are the form constraints satisfied? If both are true, the puzzle is complete. This is event-driven validation — the code doesn’t check every frame, only when something changes.

stages.title: Completion as transformation
stages.thinking: When the puzzle completes, the lines change color from cyan to green, a pulse animation plays, and the lines lock in place. Optionally, a tagged object in the map gets removed — the #plusfillhole syntax removes a floor cube, revealing what’s below. The puzzle transforms the map itself.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: Two lines, four endpoints, one geometric truth. Perpendicularity is defined by the dot product equaling zero — geometry expressed as algebra. The plus sign is not a shape you draw. It is a constraint you satisfy. The puzzle knows this about itself.
stages.code:
# @identity
# essence: ⊥ — two lines whose direction vectors have dot product zero
# desire: learner feels perpendicularity as a physical arrangement they construct
# critical_parameter: the intersection constraint — lines must cross at midpoints
# triggers: snapping all 4 endpoints to cross targets
# emerges: 90 degrees is not special until you define an inner product
# relationships: extends LineSnapPuzzleBase; contrasts with parallel_line_puzzle
# truth: perpendicularity is defined by the dot product equaling zero — geometry expressed as algebra
